claims.text: Introducing a nanohierarchical microstructure with spatial composition undulation forms an adaptive friction interface.
The nanohierarchical architecture reduces coefficient of friction across a broad temperature range.
The nanohierarchical architecture produces low wear from room temperature to approximately 800 °C.
A conventionally processed high-entropy alloy has a relatively homogeneous, coarse-grained microstructure lacking defined nanoscale features.
Rapid solidification followed by controlled annealing can induce the proposed nanoprecipitate-rich, compositionally undulating nanohierarchical architecture.
Reduced friction and wear will persist from room temperature to around 800 °C under sliding with controlled oxidation.
Nano-coupled grains or grain boundaries and nanoprecipitates evolve under frictional loading into a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer.
The adaptive interface buffers or releases frictional shear stresses in stages at lower temperatures.
At high temperature, the engineered structure promotes formation of a dense lubricious nanocrystalline glaze layer.
The dense glaze layer minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
An ultrananocrystalline near-surface layer is associated with low friction and wear in high-entropy alloys.
The adaptive interface lowers both coefficient of friction and wear rate relative to an untreated alloy.
The processed samples will have a 30–50% lower coefficient of friction than untreated samples.
The processed samples will have at least a twofold lower wear rate than untreated samples.
Untreated high-entropy alloys typically have a coefficient of friction around 0.3.
Untreated high-entropy alloys have wear rates on the order of 10^-6 mm^3/N·m or higher.
The intervention may lose effectiveness under extreme oxidation or impact loading.
The long-term stability of the adaptive interface under cyclic stress has not been established.
